answers.answer: Histones belong to the histone-fold superfamily (SCOPe class a, all-alpha; fold a.22, Histone-fold; superfamily a.22.1, Histone-fold). The histone fold is a three-helix core (alpha1-L1-alpha2-L2-alpha3) that dimerizes head-to-tail in a handshake motif. Within the superfamily, the canonical histone families (H2A, H2B, H3, H4) form H2A-H2B and H3-H4 heterodimers that assemble into the nucleosome octamer. Other proteins with the same fold are therefore related to histones at the superfamily level, not the family level. These include: (1) archaeal histone-like proteins (HMf/HTa-type), which share the fold and the dimer-forming core but are not eukaryotic histones; (2) histone-fold subunits of the general transcription factor TFIID (TAF6/TAF9-type pairs) and of the CHRAC chromatin-remodeling complex (CHRAC-15/CHRAC-16-type pairs); (3) the B and C subunits of the CCAAT-binding factor NF-Y, which dimerize through histone folds (NF-YA is not a histone-fold protein); and (4) the CENP-S/CENP-X (MHF1/MHF2-type) histone-fold pair, which is a centromere/DNA-repair complex. Some of these share only the fold and dimerization geometry with histones, so the relationship is a shared superfamily-level structural origin, not evidence of shared DNA-packaging function, sequence identity, or interchangeable function. Structure-based similarity does not transfer nucleosome-specific functions (such as octamer assembly or histone modification sites) to these proteins. Family placement within a.22.1 should be checked against the specific SCOPe release, since exact family codes and membership vary between releases and I did not verify them here.
